description: THE LAW, NOT THE READING. «The container is 1360 wide» is a fact about the window it was measured in, true here and false one drag of the mouse later — which is why comparing a layout to a mockup by measuring has never worked. This reads what the CODE DECLARED instead: how many width ceilings exist on the layout spine, which element sets the tightest one, and what content band follows from that at any window. A declaration does not move when the window does, so it can be compared with a mockup and argued about. Pass `figmaWidth` (one number off the design, e.g. 1400) and it prints the two declarations side by side plus what follows — «the mockup declares one ceiling at 1400; the code declares none at all; at 1920 the band is 1840, which is 440 wider». It NEVER says which of the two is right: that is the human's call, and an instrument that guesses it is one nobody trusts twice. VALUES THAT MOVE WITH THE WINDOW ARE REFUSED ON PURPOSE. clamp(), vw and percentages declare no single law, so they go to a `notMeasured` list with the reason instead of being resolved at the current window and printed as if they were fixed — that number would be right on this screen and wrong on the next, and indistinguishable from a real finding. Narrow boxes (a sidebar, a card) are not judged either: they are narrow by design. Read-only and free. Read `notMeasured` FIRST — a clean page and an unexamined one look identical without it.

figmaWidth.description: The mockup's own declared content width, one number. With it you get the comparison; without it you still get what the code declares.

tabId.description: Target tab (from qa_tabs); omit for the active tab

within.description: Scope to this container (a CSS selector). Omit for the whole page, which is usually what you want — the spine starts at <body>.

name: qa_width_law
title: What width the code DECLARES, not what it measured
